\section[el tiempo, llueve]{el tiempo — weather, and a word that means two things at once}

\label{lesson:ES-C30-el-tiempo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Ask a Spanish speaker \textquotedblleft{}¿qué tiempo hace?\textquotedblright{} and you're literally asking \textquotedblleft{}what time does it make?\textquotedblright{} — because \emph{tiempo} doesn't distinguish \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} from \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} the way English does.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tiempo} = both \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{time}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — from Latin \textbf{tempus}, which already covered this same double sense (English kept only the \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} half: \textbf{temporal, contemporary, tempo}). So \textbf{¿qué tiempo hace?} (\textquotedblleft{}what's the weather like?\textquotedblright{}) is literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{what time does it make}?\textquotedblright{} — context alone tells a Spanish speaker which sense is meant.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{calor} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{calor}, \textquotedblleft{}heat, warmth\textquotedblright{} $\to$ English \textbf{calorie, caloric}.
  \item \textbf{frío} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{frigidus}, \textquotedblleft{}cold\textquotedblright{} (with the middle syncopated away over time) $\to$ English \textbf{frigid, refrigerate}.
  \item \textbf{sol} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{sol}, \textquotedblleft{}sun,\textquotedblright{} unchanged $\to$ English \textbf{solar, solstice, parasol}.
\end{itemize}

You've already met \textbf{hace calor} and \textbf{hace frío} (\textquotedblleft{}it's hot/cold,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{makes} heat/cold\textquotedblright{}) back when you learned \emph{hacer} — the same \textbf{hacer} (\textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{}) that reports weather this way also covers \textquotedblleft{}sunny\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{hace sol} (\textquotedblleft{}it's sunny,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}it makes sun\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Rain} breaks the \emph{hacer} pattern entirely: \textbf{llueve} (\textquotedblleft{}it's raining\textquotedblright{}) comes from its own verb, \textbf{llover} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pluere}, \textquotedblleft{}to rain.\textquotedblright{} Recognize that \textbf{pl- $\to$ ll-} shift? It's the \textbf{same} regular sound change you met with \emph{llamar} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{clamāre}), \emph{llave} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{clāvem}), and \emph{llama} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{flamma}) — Latin \emph{cl-}, \emph{fl-}, and \emph{pl-} clusters all regularly became Spanish \emph{ll-}. So while \emph{calor/frío/sol} just need \textbf{hacer} in front of them, \emph{rain} gets its own dedicated, impersonal verb — much like English's own dedicated \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{rains}\textquotedblright{} versus \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{is} hot.\textquotedblright{}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}el tiempo\textquotedblright{} — time, or weather, depending on context{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}hace calor. hace frío. hace sol.\textquotedblright{} — it's hot/cold/sunny{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}llueve\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, its own verb, not hacer{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What two things does \textbf{el tiempo} mean, and what Latin word covers both? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Time\textquotedblright{}} and \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{}} — Latin \textbf{tempus}.) Which weather word does NOT use \emph{hacer}? (\textbf{Llueve} — \textquotedblleft{}it's raining,\textquotedblright{} its own verb \emph{llover}.) What Latin cluster did \emph{llover}'s \emph{ll-} come from, and what other word taught you this same sound change? (\textbf{pl-}, the same shift as \emph{llamar} $\leftarrow$ \emph{clamāre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
